messages.subject: How to specify the latent model for 'meb' when just a subset of the observations are with the measurement error?
parts:
Dear INLA experts

The question is on in the subject. 
To make the discussion more concrete, say, I have 100 observations, with covariate x1. x1 is a covariate with Berkson measurement error, and the other 20 have exact measure for x1.

How to specify this latent model?

Thank you in advance
Xing

Hi, Håvard

Thank you. Another three specific issues on the implementation of your suggestion.

1. This is a general question on the 'scale' argument. The default value is 1 for all 'value' arguments. My understanding is that if I set the the 'scale' argument to 95 for all 'value' arguments, the result will remain the same. Is that correct?

2. If the my understanding of the previous question is right. One strategy to implement the trick you suggested is assigning a large value, say, 10000 to the 'scale' argument to those observations without measurement error.  In contrast, assigning a same small value, say, 0.001, to those observations with measurement error. Is this plausible?

3. Strictly speaking, we need to assign infinity precision to those observations without measurement error. Can we do this like by assigning 'Inf' to corresponding 'scale' argument?

Thanks
Best,
Xing

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to specify the latent model for 'meb' when just a subset of the observations are with the measurement error?
parts:
On Sat, 2013-08-31 at 18:51 -0700, Zhao Xing wrote:
> Hi, Håvard
>
>
> Thank you. Another three specific issues on the implementation of your
> suggestion.
>
>
> 1. This is a general question on the 'scale' argument. The default
> value is 1 for all 'value' arguments. My understanding is that if I
> set the the 'scale' argument to 95 for all 'value' arguments, the
> result will remain the same. Is that correct?

apart from the the prior for the the precision, yet. if scale is 1, then
the experienced precision in the model is \tau. if the scale is 100,
then the experienced precision in the model is 100*\tau. the intention
is that the scale argument should 'vary around 1', so that you can use
that to give relative weights and then control the overall scale with
the precision. its all there in the documentation.

> 2. If the my understanding of the previous question is right. One
> strategy to implement the trick you suggested is assigning a large
> value, say, 10000 to the 'scale' argument to those observations
> without measurement error. In contrast, assigning a same small value,
> say, 0.001, to those observations with measurement error. Is this
> plausible?

assign scale 10000 to those without an error and scale=1 to thos e with.
scale=10000, means that the stdev is 1/100 of the others. you may chose
10^6 instead of'course.

> 3. Strictly speaking, we need to assign infinity precision to those
> observations without measurement error. Can we do this like by
> assigning 'Inf' to corresponding 'scale' argument?

you have to be practical, so 10^6 might be ok, or 10^8. 'Inf' is not a
good idea.

H


--

apart from the the prior for the the precision, yet. if scale is 1, then

The above is your explanation on the 'scale' argument, and I had the same understanding after reading the help documents. I have done some experiment with the data and code in your tutorials 'http://www.r-inla.org/examples/volume-1/code-for-epil-example'. The result is a little weird. There are four ways to implement the formula part, and the 1st one is from the above link.

A: formula = y ~ ClBase4 + CTrt + CBT+ ClAge + CV4 + f(Ind, model="iid") + f(rand,model="iid")
B: formula = y ~ ClBase4 + CTrt + CBT+ ClAge + CV4 + f(Ind, model="iid",scale=rep(1,59)) + f(rand,model="iid",scale=rep(1,236))
C: formula = y ~ ClBase4 + CTrt + CBT+ ClAge + CV4 + f(Ind, model="iid",scale=rep(10000,59)) + f(rand,model="iid",scale=rep(10000,236))
D: formula = y ~ ClBase4 + CTrt + CBT+ ClAge + CV4 + f(Ind, model="iid",scale=rep(1,59)) + f(rand,model="iid",scale=rep(10000,236))

I just report the fixed effect intercept in this post, as the result is lengthy. The other estimated parameters have similar patterns.
                      mean     sd     0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant kld
A: (Intercept)  1.5765 0.0762     1.4242   1.5774     1.7240   0
B: (Intercept)  1.5765 0.0762     1.4242   1.5774     1.7240   0
C: (Intercept)  1.6859 0.0310     1.6245   1.6861     1.7463   0
D: (Intercept)  1.6211 0.0763     1.4684   1.6219     1.7690   0

The inconsistencies between B and C, between B and D, between C and D, made me a little lost. Because my naive thought is that the 'scale' argument is closed in its latent environment f(), just the relative weight in that latent environment f(), and there is not interaction between different  f(), or between f() and fixed effect. If that is true, there should be not differences in the four different codes in terms of fixed effect parameter.
Is there something I missed?

Thank you,
Xing
